title: H1 – What is HRM? Roles, HR cycle and core principles

blocks.text: HRM is the management of people at work. It has a double role: strategic business partner AND employee advocate – two sides of one role (yin-yang), not a choice.
HR work spans administrative, operational and transformational (strategic) activities, increasingly supported by data analytics.
HRM is done by ALL managers, not only by the HR department – line managers run most HR practices day to day.
The individual HR cycle (Boxall & Purcell, 2008) links staffing, development, performance management, rewards and exit: practices only work if they fit together.

Core principles moved from control (monitor, narrow jobs, piece rates) to commitment (trust, teams, development). Two schools explain what works: best practice (Pfeffer, 1998) vs best fit (contingency).

The Harvard Model (Beer et al., 1984) is the stakeholder map of HRM: stakeholder interests and situational factors shape policy choices, which produce HR outcomes and long-term consequences for individuals, the organisation and society.
HR roles
Individual HR cycle (Boxall & Purcell)
children: Employer branding → staffing (job analysis, recruitment, selection, induction) → training & development, performance management, compensation & rewards → discipline & dismissal

blocks.text: Why bother?
children: Human capital theory: skills are an investment
RBV: people capabilities can be a sustained advantage
Impact on individual, environmental and societal well-being

blocks.text: Control vs commitment
children: Control: Bentham's Panopticon, Ford, call centres – value through monitoring and low labour cost
Commitment: value through trust; Japanese production model (Womack et al., 1990)

blocks.text: Best practice (Pfeffer, 1998)
children: Employment security · selective hiring · self-managed teams · high pay contingent on company performance · extensive training · reduced status differences · information sharing

blocks.text: Best fit (Jackson & Schuler, 1984)
children: Matching model: tight fit between HR and context – what works depends on the organisation

blocks.text: Harvard Model (Beer et al., 1984)
children: Stakeholder interests + situational factors → HRM policy choices (employee influence, HR flow, reward systems, work systems) → HR outcomes (commitment, competence, congruence, cost-effectiveness) → long-term consequences (individual, organisational, societal well-being), with feedback loops

blocks.text: Start with the Harvard Model as the structure of a case answer: who are the stakeholders, what is the context, which policy choice is at stake, which outcomes and consequences follow?
Use control vs commitment to diagnose the firm's philosophy – and ask whether it fits the work (routine vs knowledge work).
Use best practice vs best fit whenever a firm wants to copy one site's or one company's practices: argue for principles that travel and designs that are adapted.
Check the line manager: in most cases the HR problem is created or solved by a manager, not by the HR department.
Employees' knowledge and skills are capital: investing in them (training, selection) raises productivity and returns.
Sustained competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare and hard to imitate – people and the way they are managed can be such resources.
One bundle of HR practices improves performance in every organisation (Pfeffer, 1998).
The most effective way of managing people varies with the organisation's context; HR must fit strategy and environment.
HR outcomes: commitment, competence, congruence (of goals) and cost-effectiveness.

HR Director exercise: a fast-fashion firm (10,000 employees) must cut labour costs by 12 % while becoming a sustainability leader – which two options would you choose, and which stakeholders win or lose?
Find a modern example of a control system (algorithmic management, warehouse tracking). What are its side effects?
